subsection: 1. Origins and growth of the fascist regimes: Mussolini's Italy

notes.h: Liberal Italy and the war's legacy
notes.b: To see why fascism took hold, start with the state it replaced and what the First World War did to it. Italy's war ended in debt, grief and disappointment.
points: Before 1922 Italy was a constitutional monarchy under King Victor Emmanuel III, with an elected Chamber of Deputies. The King appointed the Prime Minister and commanded the army, which is why his decisions mattered so much in 1922 and 1943.

Italy entered the First World War in 1915 on the Allied side under the secret Treaty of London, which promised it territory from Austria-Hungary. This promise is the yardstick Italians later used to judge the peace.

The war cost heavy casualties and heavy debt, and the peace settlement gave Italy less than the Treaty of London had promised. This fed the sense of a 'mutilated victory' (vittoria mutilata, the poet D'Annunzio's phrase): Italians felt they had won the war but been cheated of the prize.

The Russian Revolution of 1917 made socialists and communists across Europe look like a real threat to property, the Church and the monarchy. Italy's propertied classes therefore watched Italian socialism with fear.

The League of Nations, set up by the peace settlement, was meant to settle disputes between states and could impose sanctions (economic penalties) on an aggressor. Its weakness in Mussolini's later foreign policy depends on this role.
notes.tip: Conditions-favouring-fascism questions reward explaining why each condition helped fascism, with an Italian example such as the mutilated victory. Do not just list the conditions.

notes.h: Conditions that favoured fascism in Italy
notes.b: Fascism grew where parliamentary government seemed weak and where fear of revolution and economic hardship had left people frightened and angry.
points: Italy had five prime ministers between 1919 and 1922 (Orlando, Nitti, Giolitti, Bonomi and Facta). Proportional representation, introduced in 1919, gave parties seats in line with their share of the vote and so produced weak coalitions dependent on the Socialists and the Catholic Popolari (the Catholic People's Party).

The Biennio Rosso (1919-1920, the 'two red years') brought strikes, peasant land seizures and factory occupations in the north. Landowners, industrialists and the middle classes feared a socialist revolution, so they were ready to back anyone who promised order.
Inflation, unemployment and food shortages added to the anger of ex-servicemen, who believed the state had failed to reward them for their sacrifice.
Fascism drew support from ex-servicemen, the lower middle class, large landowners in the Po valley and industrialists. The last two wanted an end to strikes and socialist organisation.

The poet Gabriele D'Annunzio seized Fiume with volunteers (September 1919 to December 1920). This showed the weakness of the state, which could not remove him, and gave Fascism its style: black shirts, balcony speeches, the Roman salute and mass ritual.
notes.tip: Link each condition to Italy: the mutilated victory, the Biennio Rosso, inflation and the five prime ministers. Explain how each helped fascism win support.

notes.b: Fascism was not a single fixed doctrine, but its movements shared a recognisable set of beliefs and methods. Each of these can be illustrated from Mussolini's Italy.
points: Fascism combined nationalism, a single party, a leader, violence against opponents, and hostility to socialism and liberal democracy.
Extreme nationalism: the nation is placed above the individual, so personal rights and interests count for less than the nation's greatness.
The leader principle and personality cult: power is concentrated in one leader who is said to embody the nation, and propaganda presents him as infallible and heroic.
One party and a totalitarian state: Mussolini's own formula, from a 1925 speech, was 'everything within the state, nothing outside the state, nothing against the state'.
Fascists were hostile to communism, socialism and liberal democracy, which they blamed for class conflict and national weakness.
Fascism glorified violence, war and youth, through uniformed squads and mass rallies, because it saw struggle as the way to make a strong nation.
Fascism promised corporatism, in which employers and workers would co-operate in state-controlled corporations instead of fighting a class conflict.

Comparison only: other inter-war authoritarian regimes included Horthy's Hungary (1920), Primo de Rivera's Spain (1923-30), Pilsudski's Poland (1926), Salazar's Portugal (1932) and Metaxas's Greece (1936). Most were conservative military or clerical dictatorships rather than mass fascist movements.
notes.tip: Examiners ask for characteristics with a concrete Italian example for each, such as the 1925 formula for the one-party state, the Balilla for youth or the Special Tribunal for terror.

notes.h: Key concepts: dictatorship, personality cult and totalitarianism
notes.b: Three further terms recur in every answer on Mussolini, and examiners expect them to be used precisely.
points: Dictatorship is rule by one leader or party without free elections, an independent parliament or a free press. Mussolini's rule fits this from 1925-26, once opposition parties and the free press had gone.
A personality cult presents the leader as infallible and heroic through propaganda, ritual and his image. Mussolini was Il Duce (the leader).

Totalitarianism means the state seeks to control all public and private life through one party, secret police and propaganda. The word was first used by an opponent, Giovanni Amendola, in 1923, and Mussolini then adopted it as a boast.
Italy was not fully totalitarian, because the King, the Church, the army and big business kept independent power. This is why the King was able to dismiss Mussolini in 1943.
notes.tip: Do not call Mussolini's Italy fully totalitarian without qualification. Name the King, Church, army and big business as the limits.

notes.h: Squadristi and the rise of the Fascist Party, 1919-1922
notes.b: The Fascist movement gained power through organised violence against its opponents, often tolerated by local police and army commanders.
points: Benito Mussolini, a former editor of the socialist newspaper Avanti!, founded the Fasci di Combattimento in Milan in March 1919. Its programme mixed radical and nationalist ideas, and it was a movement, not yet a party.

The squadristi were armed squads, often led by ex-servicemen, who attacked socialist offices, trade union halls and Popolari premises, especially in the Po valley and Tuscany. They were often tolerated by local police and army commanders.

Their violence was aimed at the organisations that had led the 1919-1920 unrest, so Fascism presented itself as the defender of order against socialism. Frightened property owners therefore welcomed it.

In the May 1921 election the Fascists, standing inside Liberal leader Giovanni Giolitti's electoral bloc, won 35 seats and Mussolini himself was elected. Giolitti underestimated them and believed he could control them.

Mussolini signed a Pacification Pact with socialist leaders in August 1921 to end the violence, but local squads ignored it and the pact collapsed. The movement was becoming too big for one man to restrain.
Mussolini founded the National Fascist Party (PNF) in November 1921, turning the Fasci movement into a party.
By 1922 the Fascists had taken control of many local councils in northern and central Italy. This gave them local bases of power independent of Rome.
notes.tip: Short answers ask about the Fasci and the squads. Keep the Fasci di Combattimento (a 1919 movement) separate from the National Fascist Party (PNF, founded 1921).

notes.h: The March on Rome and the first Fascist government
notes.b: The March on Rome was a show of force that persuaded the King to hand power to Mussolini rather than declare a state of siege (emergency military rule).
points: Between 27 and 30 October 1922, about 30,000 Fascists converged on Rome under four leaders, the quadrumvirs: Italo Balbo, Emilio De Bono, Cesare Maria De Vecchi and Michele Bianchi. Estimates range from about 25,000 to 30,000.
Mussolini himself waited in Milan. Prime Minister Luigi Facta asked the King for a state of siege so that the army could stop the march.

King Victor Emmanuel III refused to sign the state of siege decree, fearing civil war and doubting the army's loyalty. He invited Mussolini to form a government on 29 October, and Mussolini took office on 30 October 1922.

The March succeeded because it was a show of force and a bluff. The King handed power over legally, with the support or acceptance of conservatives, so in form it was an appointment rather than a coup.

Mussolini's first government was a coalition in which Fascists held only a minority of posts alongside Liberals, Popolari and nationalists, so he needed parliament's support. Parliament granted it emergency powers for a year in November 1922.
notes.tip: Mussolini did not march on Rome: he arrived by train after the King's invitation. A good answer explains that the King chose to hand over power because he feared civil war and revolution.

notes.b: Once in office Mussolini set about turning a minority coalition into a Fascist-controlled state. He created party and armed bodies loyal to himself and changed the electoral rules.
points: The Fascist Grand Council (December 1922) became the party's governing body, so that the party had a command centre of its own.
The Fascist militia (MVSN, the Voluntary Militia for National Security, January 1923) turned the squads into a state-paid force loyal to Mussolini rather than the King.

The Acerbo Law of 1923 gave two-thirds of the seats in the Chamber of Deputies to the list with the most votes, provided it had at least 25 per cent. Such a rule made a Fascist majority almost certain.
In the April 1924 election the Fascist-led national list won about 65 per cent of the vote (about two-thirds), in a campaign marked by intimidation and violence against opponents.
notes.tip: Do not confuse the squadristi (unofficial squads, 1920-22) with the MVSN (state-paid, 1923), or the Grand Council (a party body) with the Chamber of Deputies. State the Acerbo Law as 'most votes, provided at least 25 per cent'.

notes.h: The Matteotti murder and the move to dictatorship, 1924-1929
notes.b: The murder of a socialist deputy in 1924 threatened Mussolini's government. He survived the crisis and used it to remove parliamentary and press freedom.
points: On 30 May 1924 Giacomo Matteotti, a Socialist deputy, denounced electoral fraud and violence in the Chamber of Deputies.
Matteotti was abducted in Rome on 10 June 1924 by men connected to the Fascist squads and was murdered, so Fascist violence now reached a parliamentarian. His body was found in August.

Opposition deputies walked out of the Chamber in what became known as the Aventine Secession (1924), hoping the King would dismiss Mussolini. The King did not act, and the walkout left Mussolini free to dominate parliament.
On 3 January 1925 Mussolini told the Chamber that he accepted political responsibility for the violence, which marked the start of his open dictatorship.

The Leggi Fascistissime (1925-26) made Mussolini responsible only to the King and let him rule by decree. They banned opposition parties, censored the press, and replaced elected mayors with appointed podesta (1926).

The same laws set up a Special Tribunal for the Defence of the State (1926). Political prisoners were sent to confino (internal exile) on islands such as Lipari, and the OVRA secret police hunted opponents.
Violet Gibson, an Irishwoman and the daughter of a Lord Chancellor of Ireland, shot Mussolini in Rome on 7 April 1926 and wounded his nose. The attack was used to justify further repression.

A 1928 electoral law let the Grand Council draw up a single list of 400 candidates for voters to accept or reject. The 1929 plebiscite (a yes or no vote) approved it with about 98 per cent voting yes.
notes.tip: A chronological answer on how Mussolini built a dictatorship should run: Fasci, squads, 1921 election, March on Rome, Acerbo Law, Matteotti, 3 January 1925, Leggi Fascistissime. Do not name Matteotti's killers or give a death toll, and do not mix up the 1923 Acerbo Law with the 1928 single-list law.

notes.b: Mussolini aimed to bring industry and labour under state direction through fascist unions and corporations, so that class conflict would end. In practice the system remained more theory than reality.
points: The Rocco Law of 1926 allowed only state-recognised syndicates (unions and employers' bodies) to represent workers and employers, and it banned strikes and lockouts. Workers thus lost their independent unions.
The Charter of Labour of 1927 set out the principles of the corporate system, in which employers and workers would be organised together under the state, so that class conflict would end.

Corporations covering the main economic sectors were set up in 1934, so that each sector had a state-controlled body. In 1939 the Chamber of Deputies was replaced by the Chamber of Fasces and Corporations.
The corporate state existed largely on paper, because employers kept control of production and the corporations had little real power.
notes.tip: Keep the dates straight: the Rocco Law (1926, unions), the Charter of Labour (1927, principles) and the corporations (1934). State the policy, its aim and its result.

notes.h: The economic battles and public works
notes.b: Mussolini fought a series of publicised 'battles' to show that Fascism could make Italy strong. Most gave prestige rather than real success.
points: The Battle for Grain (from 1925) aimed at self-sufficiency in wheat by raising tariffs and expanding cereal production on poor land. It did not make Italy self-sufficient in food.
The Battle for Births, promoted from about 1927, offered rewards for large families and taxed bachelors, aiming at a bigger population for a stronger nation. The population target was not met.

Quota 90 (the Battle for the Lira) was announced in Mussolini's Pesaro speech of August 1926 and reached in 1927. It revalued the lira to 90 to the pound sterling for national prestige, but it made exports dearer, deflated the economy and cut wages.

The Pontine Marshes south of Rome were drained and resettled in the 1930s, for example, a project presented as a triumph of the regime. Autostrade (motorways) and rail electrification were other visible successes.

After the 1929 crash the state rescued banks and industry through the Institute for Industrial Reconstruction (IRI, 1933), which left the state owning a large share of banking, shipbuilding and steel.
notes.tip: For each policy give its aim and its result. Do not claim that the Battle for Births raised the birth rate, and do not give figures for wheat output or births.

notes.h: Propaganda, youth and the cult of the leader
notes.b: The regime used mass organisations, the press and film to win consent and to present Mussolini as the embodiment of the nation. Consent was backed by fear.
points: The Opera Nazionale Balilla (1926) brought boys and girls into a state youth organisation, so that children were taught fascist values from childhood. It was reorganised as the Gioventu Italiana del Littorio in 1937.
The Dopolavoro (after-work) organisation from 1925 provided, for example, sport, excursions and leisure for adult workers under fascist supervision, extending party influence into free time.
Elementary schools used a single state textbook from 1929, and university professors had to swear an oath of loyalty to the regime in 1931. Only about a dozen of over 1,200 refused.

The Istituto Luce, founded in 1924, produced newsreels and documentary films, which reached ordinary people and showed Mussolini at work, at rallies and at public works. The Ministry of Popular Culture (Minculpop, 1937) controlled the press, radio, cinema and theatre.

The cult of Il Duce used posters, photographs of him harvesting grain or bare-chested, and balcony speeches from the Palazzo Venezia in Rome, his office. Wall slogans included 'Mussolini is always right' and 'Believe, obey, fight'.

The regime used the Catholic Church and public ritual to build legitimacy, although the Church kept its own youth and press organisations. The Lateran Treaties of 11 February 1929 settled the Roman Question and created Vatican City, a success for the regime.
Consent was won by propaganda and public works, while the militia, the Special Tribunal, the OVRA and confino deterred opposition. This is why propaganda and terror must be explained together.
notes.tip: Examiners reward showing propaganda and terror working together, with named Italian bodies on each side: Istituto Luce, Minculpop and the Balilla; the militia, Special Tribunal, OVRA and confino. Do not confuse the Balilla (1926) with the Gioventu Italiana del Littorio (1937).

notes.b: Mussolini used foreign adventures to build prestige. In these years he was also wary of Hitler, and he acted first against weak neighbours.
points: The Corfu incident of August 1923 began when General Enrico Tellini of an Italian boundary commission was murdered on the Greek-Albanian border. Italy bombarded and occupied Corfu until Greece paid compensation.
Italy annexed the port of Fiume in 1924 under a treaty with Yugoslavia, which ended a long dispute left over from the peace settlement.
After Austrian Nazis murdered the Austrian Chancellor Engelbert Dollfuss in July 1934, Mussolini moved troops to the Brenner Pass, showing he opposed German control of Austria at that time.
In April 1935 Italy joined Britain and France in the Stresa Front, an agreement to resist German challenges to the peace settlement.
notes.tip: Do not confuse Corfu (1923, Greece) with Fiume (a dispute on the Yugoslav border, annexed 1924) or Albania (invaded 1939).

notes.b: The invasion of Abyssinia was Mussolini's biggest foreign gamble. It exposed the weakness of the League of Nations and pushed Italy towards Germany.
points: After the Walwal incident (December 1934), a clash on the Abyssinian border, Italy invaded Abyssinia (Ethiopia) on 3 October 1935. The attack was also revenge for Italy's defeat by Ethiopia at Adowa in 1896.
Italy used poison gas against the Abyssinians, a breach of the rules of war that shocked opinion abroad. Emperor Haile Selassie appealed to the League of Nations in 1936.
The League imposed sanctions, but they excluded oil, so they did not stop the invasion.

The Hoare-Laval Plan of December 1935, devised by the British Foreign Secretary Samuel Hoare and French Prime Minister Pierre Laval, would have given Italy much of Abyssinia. It was abandoned after public protest in Britain and France.
Addis Ababa was captured on 5 May 1936, so Victor Emmanuel III was proclaimed Emperor of Ethiopia.
notes.tip: Exams ask about Abyssinia and the League's failure. Say why the sanctions failed: oil was left out. Do not give casualty figures for the war.

notes.h: The Axis and the road to war, 1936-1940
notes.b: Isolated by the sanctions, Mussolini drew closer to Hitler. Step by step this alliance committed Italy to a war it was unprepared to fight.
points: Italy and Germany drew together after German support during the Abyssinian war. They also intervened jointly for Franco in the Spanish Civil War (1936-39).
Mussolini announced the Rome-Berlin Axis in a Milan speech on 1 November 1936. It was only an understanding between the two states, not a formal alliance.
Italy joined the Anti-Comintern Pact in 1937 and accepted the Anschluss (Germany's union with Austria) in 1938, although in 1934 it had opposed German control of Austria.
Mussolini posed as a peacemaker at the Munich Conference (September 1938), which won him prestige, and invaded Albania in April 1939.
On 22 May 1939 Italy signed the Pact of Steel, a military alliance with Germany. Yet when war began in September 1939 Italy declared itself non-belligerent.
Italy declared war on Britain and France on 10 June 1940, when France was already beaten. Defeats in Greece (invaded from October 1940) and North Africa then made Italy dependent on German help.
notes.tip: Do not confuse the Rome-Berlin Axis (1936, an understanding), the Anti-Comintern Pact (1937) and the Pact of Steel (1939, a military alliance). Finish foreign policy answers with the result: dependence on Germany and defeat.

notes.h: Collapse of the regime and the Salo republic
notes.b: Military defeats and an Allied invasion of Sicily brought the regime down in 1943. Mussolini's rule in northern Italy continued under German control until 1945.
points: Allied forces landed in Sicily on 10 July 1943, and the defeat made Fascist leaders doubt Mussolini. At a meeting on the night of 24-25 July the Fascist Grand Council passed Dino Grandi's motion to return command of the armed forces to the King.
King Victor Emmanuel III dismissed Mussolini on 25 July 1943 and had him arrested. Marshal Pietro Badoglio formed a new government.
Italy's armistice with the Allies was announced on 8 September 1943, so German forces, fearing Italy would change sides, took control of much of the north and centre.
German paratroopers and SS commandos, among them Otto Skorzeny, rescued Mussolini from a mountain hotel at Gran Sasso on 12 September 1943.

Mussolini headed the Italian Social Republic, known as the Salo Republic after its seat on Lake Garda. It was a German puppet state, and it executed his son-in-law Galeazzo Ciano and other Grand Council members at Verona in January 1944.
Mussolini and his mistress Clara Petacci were shot by partisans near Lake Como on 28 April 1945, and their bodies were displayed in Piazzale Loreto in Milan.
notes.tip: Keep the three dates in 1943 apart: 25 July (dismissal), 8 September (armistice) and 12 September (rescue). Do not confuse Grandi (proposed the motion), Ciano (executed) and Badoglio (new Prime Minister).

notes.b: Mussolini led Italy from 1922 to 1943 and was the founder and leader of the Fascist movement. Examiners ask both what he did and how others judged him.
points: Born in 1883 at Predappio in the Romagna region, he trained as a teacher, became a socialist journalist, and edited Avanti! from 1912.
He was expelled from the Socialist Party in 1914 for supporting Italian entry into the First World War. He served in the army and was wounded in 1917.

As founder of the Fasci di Combattimento (1919) and the National Fascist Party (1921), he led the movement that took power in 1922. He was Prime Minister from 1922, ruled as dictator from 1925 and was deposed in 1943.

He was a participant who shaped events: he organised the March on Rome from Milan, took personal responsibility for the violence in January 1925 and made the key decisions on Abyssinia, the Axis and entry into the war.

Contemporaries were divided. Many conservatives, the Vatican and foreign statesmen admired him for defeating socialism (Churchill praised him on a visit to Rome in 1927). Socialists, Popolari and liberals such as Giovanni Amendola, who died in 1926 after a Fascist beating, denounced his violence.

Historians differ: Renzo De Felice argued that the regime enjoyed real popular consent in 1929-1936, while Denis Mack Smith portrayed Mussolini as an opportunist and propagandist more concerned with image than with real achievement.

Many historians now regard Italian Fascism as an incomplete totalitarianism, since the King, the Church, the army and big business kept independent power. This is why the King was able to dismiss him in 1943.
notes.tip: In personality questions pair the contemporary views (admirers and opponents) with the historians' views: De Felice for consent, Mack Smith for opportunism. Do not mix up Matteotti (murdered 1924) with Amendola (died 1926).

notes.h: Assessment: achievements and limits of Mussolini's regime
notes.b: Judgements of the regime depend on whether its stability and public works are weighed against its violence, economic failures and disastrous war.
points: Achievement: Mussolini ended parliamentary rule and established a one-party state by 1926, with little open resistance for most of the 1920s.
Limit: the corporate state existed largely on paper, as employers kept control of production and the corporations had little real power.
Achievement: the Lateran Treaties of 1929 settled the Roman Question, and the Pontine Marshes scheme, the autostrade motorways and rail electrification gave the regime visible successes.
Limit: the Battle for Grain did not make Italy self-sufficient in food, and the deflationary policy of Quota 90 damaged industry and jobs.
Achievement: Italy gained territory in Abyssinia and Fiume, which the regime presented as the fulfilment of national destiny.

Limit: the Abyssinian war was costly, the alliance with Germany drew Italy into a war it was ill-prepared to fight and left it dependent on Germany, and the regime collapsed in 1943 after defeats in North Africa and Sicily.

Contemporary view: many Italians and foreign conservatives saw Mussolini as the saviour of order who had defeated Bolshevism. Later view: his regime is judged by its violence, its alliance with Hitler, the 1938 racial laws and the defeat it brought on Italy.
Overall, Mussolini was very effective at winning and keeping power (1922-1926) but much less effective at transforming the economy, society or Italy's place in the world.
notes.tip: Top answers pair achievements with limits and reach a clear verdict, such as 'effective at gaining power, ineffective at transforming Italy'. Support each point with a date or name.

keyTerms.definition: A movement and system of rule built on nationalism, a single party, the use of violence against opponents, and hostility to socialism and liberal democracy.
Rule by one leader or party that holds power without free elections, an independent parliament or a free press.
The promotion of a leader as an infallible and heroic figure, shown through propaganda, rituals and his image in public life.

A system in which the state seeks to control every aspect of public and private life through a single party, secret police and propaganda; the term was coined by Mussolini's opponent Giovanni Amendola in 1923 and then adopted by Mussolini himself.
Armed Fascist squads, often of ex-servicemen, that attacked socialist and Catholic organisations in Italy between 1920 and 1922.
The Fascist show of force of 27 to 30 October 1922, after which King Victor Emmanuel III appointed Mussolini Prime Minister.
The 1923 electoral law that gave two-thirds of the seats in the Chamber of Deputies to the list winning at least 25 per cent of the vote.
The fascist model of economic organisation in which employers and workers were grouped into state-recognised corporations rather than independent unions.
The fighting groups founded by Mussolini in Milan in March 1919, which became the basis of the National Fascist Party.
D'Annunzio's phrase for Italy's sense that it had won the First World War but been cheated of the territory promised in the Treaty of London (1915).
The withdrawal of opposition deputies from the Chamber of Deputies after Matteotti's murder in 1924, which failed when the King refused to dismiss Mussolini.
Mussolini's revaluation of the lira to 90 to the pound sterling (1926-27), a prestige policy that deflated the Italian economy.

factCards.definition: Issued in 1927, it set out the principles of the corporate system in which workers and employers were organised under the state.
